title: Yes means yes
hook: don't laugh much or loudly, and avoid swearing oaths when you can (Enchiridion 33)

segments.voice: Yesterday: the first rule of section thirty-three, silence by default, and not about people. Your line was mostly quiet. Did you let a piece of gossip pass? Day three hundred sixty-six.

I swear I'll be there. I swear on my mother. Hand on heart, I promise. We stack these up when we want to be believed, and the funny thing is, the more we pile on, the less sure everyone gets. Someone who says I swear three times in a sentence is usually the one you double-check. Section thirty-three keeps going with its sketch of a person of character, and today it gets to two small habits: how you laugh, and how you promise. Today: yes means yes.
screen: `I SWEAR. I SWEAR ON MY MOTHER.` → `THE MORE WE PILE ON, THE LESS SURE.` → `YES MEANS YES.`

segments.voice: First, laughter. Don't laugh much, Epictetus says, or at many things, or without restraint. That can sound grim, so look closely. He isn't banning joy. The worry, across this section, is the kind of laughing that runs away with a person: laughing to fit in, laughing at someone, laughing so loudly that you're no longer really there. A smile you mean is still in your power. A roar to impress the room may not be. Second, oaths. Refuse to swear an oath, he says, altogether if you can, and if you can't, as far as you can. In his world, people swore by the gods constantly, in business, in court, in ordinary talk. Third, why. If your plain word is good, an oath adds nothing. If your plain word isn't good, an oath won't fix it. Piling on swears is a quiet admission that a simple yes isn't enough. So the Stoic aims to be the kind of person whose yes is the whole promise. Fourth, a neighbor who said something close. In the Sermon on the Mount, in the King James Bible, Jesus says: "But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay." Christians have taken that in different ways. Quakers and some Mennonite and Amish communities decline to swear oaths at all and affirm instead. Many other Christians take oaths in court and office and read the verse as being about honesty. That's why the United States Constitution lets a president swear, or affirm. Two traditions, each in its own house, arriving at the same plain picture: a word that doesn't need help.
screen: `DON'T LAUGH MUCH, OR WITHOUT RESTRAINT.` · `REFUSE OATHS, AS FAR AS YOU CAN.` · `A GOOD WORD NEEDS NO OATH.` · `YEA, YEA; NAY, NAY.` · then, large: `YES MEANS YES.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Think of one promise you've made recently, small or large. I'll call you back. I'll finish it by Friday. I'll be there. Picture the person you made it to. Now, without adding a single I swear, just decide to keep it. Feel how plain that is: no drama, no extra words, just a yes that holds. If there's a promise you can't keep, picture yourself telling them so, simply. The bell holds the time.
Yes means yes. Epictetus' advice to refuse oaths as far as you can, and to let your plain word carry the promise. Today's word.
Your line: yes means yes. Keep one promise today without swearing, stacking, or hand-on-heart. Just say yes, and do it. Day three hundred sixty-six.

howItsDone: Some people on a Stoic path avoid oaths and emphatic promises and try to keep their plain word instead; Quakers and some other Christian communities affirm rather than swear.

notes: Enchiridion 33.4–5 paraphrased: laughter not much, nor at many things, nor unrestrained; refuse an oath altogether if possible, if not, as far as possible. Section numbering within 33 varies by edition; confirm.
The explanation of why (a good word needs no oath) is an interpretive gloss, not Epictetus' stated reason. Confirm it is fair.
Quakers, and some Mennonite and Amish communities, decline oaths and affirm; many other Christians take oaths. Confirm the description is fair and unranked.
U.S. Constitution Art. II, Sec. 1 presidential oath: 'swear (or affirm)'. Confirm.
